_note: Ranking the World's Most Vulgar Languages: ranked by the number of words tagged 'vulgar' in the English Wiktionary (Category:<Language> vulgarities, counted 2026-10-18, cache/vulgar_counts.json). One signature swear word per language, spoken by a real Lingua Libre recording where one exists.
title: Ranking the World's Most Vulgar Languages

items.name: German
cards: Germans swear with the toilet, not with sex: 'Scheiße' does the job of half the English dictionary.
The insults are oddly musical. 'Arschgeige' is an arse violin, 'Backpfeifengesicht' a face that needs a slap.

items.name: Finnish
cards: Finland's favourite swear word is a pagan god: 'perkele' comes from Perkūnas, the Baltic god of thunder. Christianity turned him into the devil.
The rolled r is the point. Finns say a long 'perrrkele' is the most Finnish sound there is.

items.name: Portuguese
items.lit: the ship's crow's nest (and the c-word)
cards: Sailors called the lookout at the top of the mast the 'caralho', so 'go to the caralho' sounded like a punishment. A nice story, but linguists say the rude meaning came first.
Brazil and Portugal swear with the same words and different favourites: 'porra' every second sentence in Brazil, 'foda-se' in Lisbon.

items.name: French
cards: In the south of France 'putain' is punctuation: surprise, joy, anger, or simply the start of a sentence.
'Merde' is the other classic, and actors say it to each other for good luck, the way English says 'break a leg'.

items.name: Chinese
cards: Chinese swears with your family. The classic insult targets your mother, the strong version all eighteen generations of your ancestors.
'Kào' means 'to lean' and sounds like the real thing, so it became the version you can say in front of your parents.

items.name: Russian
cards: Russian 'mat' is a whole grammar: four root words produce hundreds of nouns, verbs and adjectives. Since 2014 it is banned in films, theatre and media.
'Blin' means pancake. It is what you say instead, the way English says 'sugar'.

items.name: Polish
cards: Poles joke that 'kurwa' is a comma. It is a noun, an interjection, a filler and a sigh, several times per sentence.
Add 'mać' (mother) and you get 'kurwa mać', the full-strength version.

items.name: Italian
cards: Italians put a pig in front of anything to curse it: pig misery, pig Madonna, pig God.
That last kind, the 'bestemmia', is the real taboo: it is banned on television and was a criminal offence until 1999.

items.name: Spanish
cards: Spain swears with the church: 'hostia' is the communion wafer, and it means 'damn', 'wow' and 'a punch in the face'.
The famous formula is 'me cago en…' (I shit on…), followed by anything: the sea, the milk, or God.

items.name: English
cards: In 1914 a single 'not bloody likely' on a London stage made the newspapers. Today it is the mildest word on this list.
Why so many? The dictionary knows its own language best: Wiktionary tags five times more English words as vulgar than any other language. Take the gold with a grain of salt.
